title: When Institutions Make Themselves the End
body: A question that looks absurd in hindsight
On March 7, 1936, Hitler ordered thirty thousand German troops into the demilitarized Rhineland. It openly violated the Treaty of Versailles and directly challenged the entire postwar order.

We now know that those troops had orders to withdraw immediately if the French made any military response. Hitler himself later admitted that the forty-eight hours after the advance into the Rhineland were the most nerve-racking of his life.

But France and Britain took no military action, and the League of Nations produced no response strong enough to halt the advance. The German army was not yet ready to fight the French army; a determined military response might have forced it to withdraw. That does not mean we can assert that all the later war and catastrophe could thereby have been avoided.

Looking back, this seems almost incomprehensible. The signals were all there: rearmament, withdrawal from the League, the Nuremberg Laws. Almost every step told the world what this regime intended. Why did nobody stop it?

The usual explanations are weak leaders, shortsighted politicians, and populations weary of war. Each has some force, but each explains institutional behavior through individual psychology. The real question is not “Why was Chamberlain so naïve?” It is why an entire institutional order, the League of Nations, collective security, and national democracies alike, failed at every decisive point over six years to stop a regime that had plainly declared its intentions.
The answer is not simply that institutions were too weak. It is more unsettling than that.
The design logic of Versailles
To understand why institutions failed, we first need to understand the logic by which they were designed.

The architects of the Versailles settlement were no fools. Clemenceau, Lloyd George, and Wilson, the Big Three at the Paris Peace Conference, were among their countries' shrewdest political minds. Their problem was clear: how could they ensure that Germany could not wage war again? Their answer was equally clear: weaken its military, drain its economic resources through reparations, reduce its strategic space through territorial changes, and constrain it morally through the war guilt clause.

Technically, these measures worked. Germany in the 1920s really was unable to wage war. But the plan answered an engineering question, “How do we stop this machine from running?” It did not answer a human question: “How do we make the tens of millions living in this society feel that the peace settlement is fair to them too?”

The difference is that the first question takes the system's security as its end; the second takes the condition of human beings. The architects of Versailles cared whether the machine of European order would run smoothly. How people inside the machine felt was not part of the equation.

The deeper problem was that the institutional order they created was designed from the start around “preserving the system itself” rather than “serving people.” That design logic shaped the pattern of its later responses.
The League of Nations: designed not to act
The League's ideas were good: collective security, multilateral consultation, rules instead of force. Had those ideas truly been carried out, the Second World War would probably not have happened.

But the League faced a fundamental contradiction from birth. Its authority depended on the participation of the great powers, whose condition for participating was that it must not genuinely constrain them. The United States never joined at all: the Senate rejected Wilson's life's work. Britain and France joined, but treated the League as an instrument of their own interests, not a set of standards governing their own behavior.
The League thus became something it could not acknowledge: an institution whose first priority was to perpetuate its own existence.

In 1931, Japan invaded Manchuria. What did the League do? It sent a commission of inquiry, which spent a year producing a report mildly critical of Japan. Japan then withdrew from the League. That was that.

In 1935, Italy invaded Abyssinia, today's Ethiopia. This time, the League did vote for sanctions, but deliberately left oil off the list. Britain and France feared that genuinely effective sanctions would push Mussolini toward Hitler.

The two cases reveal the same logic. At each decisive moment, the League chose self-preservation over honoring its commitments. Enforcing collective security, sanctioning an aggressor or, if necessary, using force, meant that the great powers had to accept costs and risks. Once they began calculating those costs, keeping the League “in existence” proved much cheaper than fulfilling its “promise.”

Where did the Chinese people of Manchuria and the African people of Abyssinia stand in this calculation? Nowhere. They were not variables in the equation. The only variable was the cost of keeping the system alive.

A League that kept holding meetings without enforcing its resolutions was an optimal outcome for the system. For people facing invasion, it was a disaster. But the system did not concern itself with the latter, because its end was itself.
Appeasement: an apparently rational calculation

Munich, September 1938. Chamberlain handed Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland to Hitler and returned with a piece of paper promising “peace for our time.” Posterity has treated it as a textbook case of folly and weakness.

But put yourself in Chamberlain's position, not to defend him but to understand the institutional logic. He faced an arithmetic problem. On one side stood the Sudetenland and its three million German-speaking inhabitants. Hitler claimed that this was all he wanted; give it to him and he would be satisfied. On the other side, refusal meant war. Britain had not completed rearmament. The mire of the First World War remained vivid in public memory. The empire's defensive commitments were already overstretched worldwide.
From the perspective of maintaining the system, the calculation had a “rational” answer: exchange three million people for peace. Not a good answer, but a calculable one.

“Calculable” is where the trouble begins. In this arithmetic, the Sudetenland's three million inhabitants were numbers, weights on one side of an equation. They were not three million people with names, families, fears, and hopes. They were a variable the system could move around to keep itself functioning.

Chamberlain was not an evil man. He genuinely wanted to avoid war and genuinely believed that sacrificing a small part could save the whole. That is precisely the problem. Once an institution becomes accustomed to treating people as variables, “sacrifice some people to sustain the system” remains a permanent option. Once that option exists, the only question is “Who gets sacrificed this time?”

Six months after Munich, German forces occupied Bohemia and Moravia, Slovakia became a state dependent on Germany, and Czechoslovakia was further dismembered. Chamberlain's arithmetic proved wrong. But even if the answer had been right, even if Hitler really had stopped at the Sudetenland, the logic of the calculation would still have been unjust. It had already established a principle: people can be traded.
Weimar democracy: procedure swallowed its purpose

Institutional failure was not confined to international affairs. Within Germany, the Weimar Republic's democratic institutions also failed to prevent catastrophe. The manner of their failure was even more disturbing: legal forms combined with violent coercion to become instruments for destroying democracy.

The Nazi Party became the largest party in parliament through elections. Hitler was appointed chancellor through a constitutional procedure. But the seizure of power that followed can no longer be called the normal operation of democratic procedures. Opponents were arrested, legislators were excluded from the chamber, and armed men intimidated those present. The Enabling Act retained the form of a parliamentary vote, but it was passed under these conditions.

Technically, the Weimar Constitution was among Europe's most advanced democratic constitutions. Proportional representation gave diverse voices a place, civil-rights provisions protected individual freedom, and emergency provisions offered flexibility in a crisis. It contained progressive commitments to rights, alongside emergency powers open to abuse.
Those commitments did not stop dictatorship. Emergency powers, political deals, and violent coercion together dismantled the institutions that were supposed to protect people.
What went wrong? Legal forms did not automatically protect democracy. Combined with coercion, they instead provided a cloak for dictatorship.

The question becomes more specific: when safeguards for rights have already been dismantled, yet people inside institutions still treat the surviving forms as grounds for obedience, procedure can become an instrument for destroying its own purpose.

On February 28, 1933, the day after the Reichstag fire, Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree, suspending several crucial constitutional guarantees of civil liberty. In late March, the Enabling Act gave Hitler's government the power to legislate without parliament. Emergency powers supplied a legal form. They did not turn the repression of opponents, the deprivation of rights, and the intimidation of legislators into the normal operation of democracy.
The tools of a democratic order were used to dismantle democracy itself. The legal forms that remained could not conceal the violence and the stripping away of rights.

Here lies a deep danger. A democracy that watches only whether its formal machinery is still running may miss the destruction of the rights that sustain it. Institutions are needed to resist attack, but they must also hold fast to their purpose of protecting people. Weimar failed to hold that line.
Why institutions become like this

A pattern should now be clear. Versailles prioritized the system's security over people's condition. The League prioritized its own survival over making collective security real. Appeasement prioritized preserving order over the fate of those sacrificed. Weimar's institutional safeguards failed to withstand the simultaneous erosion of procedures and rights.
At each crucial moment, each institution chose to preserve itself rather than protect people.

This did not happen because everyone inside those institutions was bad. Chamberlain was not a bad man. Nor was the League's secretary-general. Most Weimar legislators were not bad people either. Many sincerely believed that they were doing the right thing. The issue lay not with their character, but with the logic.

Once established, an institution acquires an instinct for self-preservation: protect its continued existence, maintain its operation, avoid actions that might bring about its collapse. Nobody has to deliberately instill this instinct. It is what an institution naturally does as a system. Just as an organism avoids harming itself, an institution avoids choices that threaten its survival.

In many situations, however, “protecting people” conflicts directly with “preserving the institution.” Sanctioning Japan might break up the League; refusing Hitler might mean war; banning the Nazi Party might violate the constitution. At each juncture, protecting people looked more costly and risky than preserving the institution. Each time, the institution chose itself.
This was not an institutional malfunction. It was the result of institutions operating “successfully” according to their own logic.
The most unsettling part

We are accustomed to thinking of institutions as instruments for protecting people. Constitutions safeguard rights, international law preserves peace, multilateral bodies prevent aggression. All true. Institutions often do protect people.

But institutions are also doing something else: preserving themselves. When “protecting people” and “preserving themselves” conflict, their default is the latter. Perhaps not every time, but in those decisive cases, it certainly was.

What follows? Institutions cannot be trusted unconditionally. Not because they are evil, but because they have their own logic of survival, which does not naturally coincide with treating people as ends. Sometimes the two overlap; sometimes they conflict. When they conflict, expecting institutions automatically to choose the human side is a dangerous kind of innocence.
The twenty years from 1919 to 1939 show the cost of that innocence. Every institution was functioning normally. None was protecting people.
deck: Versailles, the League, appeasement, and Weimar: what happens when institutions preserve themselves at the expense of the people they serve.
